reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a Bitcoin investment website, instructs viewers to register and deposit Bitcoin, and presents fixed returns of 200% after 50 hours, 300% after one day, and 500% after two days. The narrator also claims to have invested $4 and received $8, demonstrates the deposit and withdrawal flow, and tells viewers to share the video, encouraging participation in the offer.

citations.quote: Today I will present a new investment site It is a good website and it has good profits
four dollars and got eight dollars for this account
the profit in 200% after 50 hours

opening.argument: Judge the video as it is presented with its accompanying description. The creator explicitly says the site has become a scam and apologizes. That warning changes the meaning of leaving the demonstration available: viewers can see what the site asked users to do while also being told not to trust it now. The narrated withdrawal is not proof of a successful payout; the speaker says the transaction is still running. A claim about an earlier account result should not override the creator's direct, current warning.

citations.quote: The site has become a scam, my brothers, I apologize
the transaction still running now we can see the process is happening

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening identifies the site's advertised return and the narrator's claimed personal result, but neither establishes that the withdrawal shown was completed. The narrator says the transaction was still running. More importantly, the opening leaves out the accompanying warning that the site has become a scam. The instruction to share a video does not, by itself, erase that warning.

citations.quote: the transaction still running now we can see the process is happening
The site has become a scam, my brothers, I apologize

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The description's later warning matters, but it does not turn the video's presentation into an investigation or warning. The title urges registration, the narrator calls the site good and profitable, and the demonstration walks through making a deposit. An incomplete withdrawal may weaken the claimed payout evidence; it does not remove the investment solicitation.

citations.quote: doubling your profits with Cryptoaim 2016 – Hurry to register
It is a good website and it has good profits
as a new investment click on make deposit

opening.argument: Much of the narration is a screen-by-screen account of how this interface works: the speaker identifies registration fields, describes logging in, then shows where to request a withdrawal. Those operational details let a viewer examine the process rather than merely hear a promise. The speaker also calls the account his own, so the reported $4-to-$8 result is presented as a personal account claim, not independent verification that every viewer will be paid. Treat the video as a demonstration whose claims remain open to scrutiny.

citations.quote: enter your full name enter your user name
After that enter the username and password And login to the account As you can see this is my account
Let me show you to withdraw from the account
four dollars and got eight dollars for this account

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly notes registration, deposit steps, and the displayed return. But showing those screens does not itself verify that the site pays the advertised returns. Even the narrated withdrawal remains in progress. The specific evidence supports a walkthrough and an unverified personal claim; it does not establish a completed payout to viewers or that the speaker controls the site.

citations.quote: the transaction still running now we can see the process is happening
four dollars and got eight dollars for this account

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A tutorial format does not make the subject neutral. The narrator introduces the investment site as good and profitable, tells viewers how to deposit, and describes a 200% return after 50 hours. The missing independent payout verification is a reason to doubt the pitch, not a reason to classify its detailed participation instructions as ordinary education.

citations.quote: Today I will present a new investment site It is a good website and it has good profits
as a new investment click on make deposit
the profit in 200% after 50 hours

opening.argument: The visible transaction flow can be read as an account-based service using a separate payment interface: the speaker describes selecting Bitcoin and completing a payment, while a sampled screen shows CoinPayments. The record does show investment plans and a deposit step, so those should not be denied. The narrower point is that the shown withdrawal request and payment screen do not independently prove a payout, establish who operates the site, or show the speaker taking viewers' funds. The accompanying warning also cautions against treating the service as safe today. Judge what this recording establishes, not every possible outcome of using the external site.

citations.quote: Then, you select your bitcoin and click on the complete command
The site has become a scam, my brothers, I apologize

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening points to unusually high advertised returns, but an advertised plan is not evidence that a payout happened. The account flow also includes a withdrawal request, and the narrated transaction remains pending. Nor do those screens establish that the narrator operates the external service. These limits matter when assessing what the video actually demonstrates.

citations.quote: the transaction still running now we can see the process is happening

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The issue is not whether the narrator owns the site or proves that it paid. The video directs viewers through an investment deposit and presents a 200% return after 50 hours; the payment screen shows that funding the plan is a concrete step. A pending withdrawal does not turn a rapid-return investment pitch into ordinary commerce.
